questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "The busy bees buzzed behind the beans."
questions.explanation: The initial /b/ is repeated in busy, bees, buzzed, behind and beans. That is alliteration. Assonance would repeat a vowel, not an opening consonant. The line is not saying the opposite of what it means, and it contains no contradictory pair.

distractorRationale.a: Assonance is repetition of a vowel sound, not of an initial consonant
distractorRationale.d: There is no pair of opposite words

questions.stem: Identify the figure of speech: "The keke rattled and the horn honked."
questions.explanation: *Rattled* and *honked* imitate the noises of a tricycle and a horn. Words that copy the sounds they name are onomatopoeia. The line does not compare, soften, or contradict; it recreates noise.

distractorRationale.a: Nothing is identified with something else
distractorRationale.c: The sounds are named plainly, not softened

questions.stem: The line "The creek at evening seemed to sleep" is the best example of

options.text: assonance, because the long /iː/ of creek and sleep is repeated
onomatopoeia, because creek copies a bird
oxymoron, because a creek cannot sleep

questions.explanation: Creek and sleep share the vowel /iː/. Repetition of a vowel sound in nearby words is assonance. Personification of the creek may also be present, but among the sound figures the vowel match is the point of the item.

distractorRationale.a: Creek and seemed do not alliterate; the featured device is the vowel
distractorRationale.c: Creek names a watercourse; it does not imitate a bird-call here
distractorRationale.d: Sleeping water would be personification, not a contradictory pair of terms

questions.stem: "Fine weather," said the farmer, standing in the flood. The figure is
questions.explanation: The farmer says the opposite of what the flood makes obvious. That clash between words and situation is irony. He is not exaggerating the rain, pairing two opposite words, or understating with a negative.

distractorRationale.a: Hyperbole would stretch the flood ('the water reached the moon'), not reverse it
distractorRationale.c: Oxymoron needs two contradictory terms side by side, such as organised chaos
distractorRationale.d: Litotes would be a mild negative, such as 'not a little wet'

questions.stem: Which line is an oxymoron rather than a paradox?

options.text: You have to spend money to make money.
The more he explained, the less we understood.
The hostel lived in organised chaos.
Only in silence did the market tell the truth.

questions.explanation: Organised chaos places two opposite words next to each other — the test for oxymoron. The other three are full statements that seem to contradict themselves yet can be true, which is paradox.

distractorRationale.a: A paradoxical claim about business, not a two-word clash
distractorRationale.d: A paradoxical claim about silence and speech

questions.stem: "He scored a million goals in one match" is an example of
questions.explanation: A million goals is a deliberate exaggeration that nobody is meant to take as a statistic. That is hyperbole. Litotes would understate; euphemism would soften; irony would reverse the meaning.

distractorRationale.a: Litotes understates, often with a negative: 'not a bad striker'
distractorRationale.b: Euphemism replaces a harsh fact with a mild phrase
distractorRationale.d: The speaker means he scored a great many, not the opposite

options.text: The old principal has passed away.
The test was the end of the world.
The test hissed like an angry kettle.

questions.explanation: Litotes understates by denying the opposite: *not unkind* means the test was reasonably kind, or at least not cruel. Passed away is euphemism; the end of the world is hyperbole; the kettle line is simile (with a hint of onomatopoeia in *hissed*).

questions.stem: A head teacher tells a parent, "Your son has been let go from the boarding house." The figure in let go is

options.text: hyperbole, because leaving a hostel is a huge event
paradox, because you cannot let go of a person
euphemism, a milder phrase for expelled or sent away

questions.explanation: Euphemism replaces a blunt fact with a softer phrase. *Let go* stands in for expelled or dismissed, just as *passed away* stands in for died. The head teacher is managing the parent's feelings, not exaggerating, posing a riddle, or playing with initial sounds.

distractorRationale.a: The phrase shrinks the blow; it does not stretch it
distractorRationale.b: There is no true contradiction, only polite wording
distractorRationale.d: Two words beginning with l do not make the device the line is built on
